newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear policy left largely intact by reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear policy left largely intact by reform.

text.p: Japan's nuclear research firm will be streamlined and taken over by a new body, a government panel said on Wednesday, but analysts say little will change within the much-maligned organisation in terms of its core strategy and operations.
"PNC (Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp) is only giving up what has already been established commercially, said Naoaki Usui, a Tokyo-based Nuclear Industry analyst.
"The government has managed to maintain both its fast-breeder reactor programme and its fuel recycling programme," he added.

The government panel, established in April after a series of nuclear accidents and cover-up attempts undermined confidence in the PNC, has been discussing ways to reform the state firm for the past three months.

At its sixth and final meeting on Wednesday, the panel finalised earlier plans that a new entity take over PNC operations, and that certain peripheral entities within the firm be done away with or sold to private interests.
Included in this category are the PNC units which oversee uranium exploration in foreign countries and uranium enrichment domestically, both of which will be privatised.
On the chopping block is the Fugen advanced thermal reactor on the Sea of Japan Coast, as well as a prototype uranium enrichment plant in western Japan.

Left intact, however, are the firm's controversial fast-breeder reactor and radioactive waste management system -- the centrepieces of Japan's ambitious nuclear recycling programme and origin of much of the calamity which has befallen Japan's nuclear program over the last two years.
Problems began when the Monju prototype fast-breeder reactor was shut in December1995 due to a coolant leakage accident.
It was later revealed that plant officials edited video footage of the accident before making it public, in an effort to conceal the extent of the damage.
Then, in March this year, a fire and explosion at its sole nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, operated also by PNC, exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
The accident was followed by revelations that an original report on the accident was falsified.
The incidents drew intense public scrutiny and criticism of the firm, both in Japan and abroad, for its failure to quickly and accurately report nuclear accidents.

Analysts say the appointment of supervisors from outside of PNC to take the reins of the firm is a significant step, aimed at restoring public confidence in Japan's nuclear energy programme as a whole.
Others say the reform is insufficient.

"The restructuring of PNC should have been preceded by a review of the government's own nuclear policy and more public discussion," Jinzaburo Takagi, executive director of Japan's Citizens' Nuclear Information Centre said in a statement.
